title: Deriving gravitational potential energy
prior_knowledge_summary: Work done is the product of force and displacement in the direction of the force.
The weight of a mass m in a uniform gravitational field is mg.
At constant speed, the resultant force is zero, so a steady upward lifting force equals the weight when resistive forces are negligible.
new_learning: Connect lifting work to an increase in gravitational potential energy.
Derive the formula for gravitational potential energy change from W = Fs.
Explain why vertical height change, rather than path length, determines the gravitational potential energy change in a uniform field.
Interpret the sign of the energy change when a mass rises or falls.

blocks.title: Two routes to the same shelf
content: A 10 kg crate can be lifted straight up to a shelf or pushed along a long smooth ramp to the same shelf. The ramp route is much longer. Does the crate gain more gravitational potential energy on the ramp?

The route changes the force and distance used by the person, but both routes finish with the crate at the same vertical height. We need a way to connect work done with the energy stored because of height.

figure.purpose: Create a prediction about path length and vertical height
figure.brief: Show one crate reaching the same shelf by a short vertical lift and a longer smooth ramp. Mark the same vertical height change on both routes. Do not show an energy answer.
figure.alt_text: A crate reaches the same shelf by a vertical lift and by a longer ramp, with equal vertical height changes.

blocks.title: What gravitational potential energy means
blocks.accepted_definition: energy stored by a mass because of its position or height in a gravitational field
content: Gravitational potential energy is not a force. It is energy associated with where a mass is in a gravitational field.
We usually calculate a change in this energy. The chosen zero level can move, but the energy change between two heights does not.

figure.purpose: Separate energy from force and show the role of a reference level
figure.brief: Show a mass at lower and upper positions beside a freely chosen zero-height line. Label position, height and energy store, while keeping force arrows separate.
figure.alt_text: A mass is shown at two heights above a chosen reference level, separating position energy from force.

blocks.title: Why constant speed makes the force clear
content: Imagine raising a mass vertically at constant speed with negligible resistance. Its acceleration is zero, so the upward lifting force has the same magnitude as its downward weight.

The weight formula to remember is W = mg. Here W means weight in newtons, m is mass in kilograms and g is gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram. In the derivation, write the lifting force as F = mg to avoid confusing weight W with work done W.

If the mass accelerates, the lifting force need not equal mg. The formula for gravitational potential energy change still describes the height change, but the simple lifting-work argument must then separate energy going into motion.

figure.purpose: Show why the lifting force equals mg in the derivation
figure.brief: Draw a mass moving upward at constant speed with equal upward F and downward mg arrows. Add a small zero-resultant-force note without introducing later energy equations.
figure.alt_text: A mass moving upward at constant speed has equal upward lifting force and downward weight.

blocks.title: Build the formula from work done
content: Remember the work formula W = Fs. F is the force in newtons and s is displacement in metres in the direction of that force.
For a steady vertical lift, F = mg and s = Δh. Substitution gives W = (mg)(Δh) = mgΔh.
The work done against gravity is stored as an increase in gravitational potential energy. Therefore ΔE_P = W = mgΔh.

In ΔE_P = mgΔh, ΔE_P is the change in gravitational potential energy in joules, m is mass in kilograms, g is gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram and Δh is vertical height change in metres.
The unit check is kg × N kg⁻¹ × m = N m = J. This confirms that the right side has the unit of energy.

figure.purpose: Make every substitution in the derivation visible
figure.brief: Use a four-step hand-drawn chain: W = Fs, F = mg, s = Δh, then ΔE_P = mgΔh. Include symbol meanings and a separate unit check.
figure.alt_text: A four-step derivation connects work done to the gravitational potential energy change formula.

blocks.title: A steady lift
content: A 12.0 kg lighting unit is raised 2.40 m at constant speed in a uniform field where g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹.
The lifting force is F = mg = 12.0 × 9.81 = 117.72 N. The work done is W = FΔh = 117.72 × 2.40 = 282.528 J.
Using the derived formula directly gives ΔE_P = mgΔh = 12.0 × 9.81 × 2.40 = 282.528 J = 283 J to three significant figures.
The two routes agree because the lifting work has become gravitational potential energy. The unit check also gives N m, which is J.

figure.purpose: Model a complete derivation-based calculation and independent check
figure.brief: Show an annotated lighting unit rising 2.40 m beside two calculation columns: work route and energy formula route, both meeting at 283 J.
figure.alt_text: A lighting unit rises 2.40 metres, with work and energy calculations both giving 283 joules.

blocks.title: Why the longer ramp does not store more gravitational energy
content: It feels reasonable that a longer route must create a larger gravitational potential energy change because W = Fs contains a distance. The mistake is using the long path with the full weight mg as if both pointed along the path.
On a smooth shallow ramp, the force needed along the ramp is smaller than mg while the distance is longer. Their product gives the same work as mg multiplied by the vertical rise.

For a 5.00 kg crate reaching a shelf 1.60 m higher, ΔE_P = 5.00 × 9.81 × 1.60 = 78.5 J whether the smooth route is vertical or sloping. The scientific model uses the vertical height change, not the path length.

figure.brief: Compare a short steep route and a long shallow route to the same height. Use force-length rectangles of equal area without showing trigonometry or copying an official diagram.
figure.alt_text: Two routes to the same height pair a larger force with a shorter distance and a smaller force with a longer distance.

blocks.title: Rising, falling and the sign of the change
content: Height change means final height minus initial height. If a mass rises, Δh is positive and its gravitational potential energy increases.
If a mass falls, Δh is negative and ΔE_P is negative. The negative sign says the gravitational energy store has decreased. It does not mean the object has impossible negative energy.
For a 3.0 kg mass falling 0.50 m, Δh = -0.50 m and ΔE_P = 3.0 × 9.81 × (-0.50) = -14.7 J. The store loses 14.7 J.

blocks.title: The derivation in one clean chain
content: Start with W = Fs. For a steady vertical lift in a uniform field, replace F by mg and s by Δh. Identify the work done against gravity as the change in gravitational potential energy. This gives ΔE_P = mgΔh.
Check four things: the field is treated as uniform, Δh is vertical height change, the sign matches rising or falling, and the units reduce to joules.
The next practice set asks you to reconstruct this reasoning, not merely quote its final line.
